questions.q: Roughly what out-of-sample R² on next-period return prediction is often considered a strong, usable result in quantitative finance?
options: Around 0.40 (40%)
Around 0.95 (95%)
R² is never used to evaluate financial models
questions.explain: Because markets are close to efficient, easily exploitable patterns get traded away, leaving only a faint signal. An R² of 1-2% is often genuinely strong; much higher usually signals a bug or leakage.

questions.q: A brand-new model reports an out-of-sample R² of 0.40 on next-day stock returns. What should you suspect first?
options: That you've made a real breakthrough and should start trading on it immediately
That the model is simply more powerful than linear regression
A bug such as look-ahead bias, a leaked label, or misaligned data
That the stock market is unusually predictable this year
questions.explain: A result far above the typical 1-2% range for financial returns is a red flag for leakage or a data error, not a sign of genuine predictive skill.

questions.q: What does 'non-stationarity' mean in the context of financial markets?
options: Prices never move
The statistical properties of the data, such as volatility and correlations, change over time
The data has no noise at all
Trading volume is always zero
questions.explain: Non-stationarity means the data-generating process itself shifts over time -- volatility regimes change, correlations between assets drift, and factor strength varies.

options: A technique for regularizing linear regression
The gradual weakening or disappearance of a real predictive signal as more participants discover and trade on it
A method for detecting look-ahead bias
The natural decline in a stock's price over time
questions.explain: Alpha decay describes how a genuine, working signal can lose its predictive power once enough market participants find and exploit it, crowding out the edge.

questions.q: Why does this course devote an entire later chapter to validation rigor (walk-forward and purged cross-validation)?
options: Because validation is only relevant to deep learning models
Because low signal combined with a constantly shifting data-generating process makes it unusually easy to mistake a lucky or leaked result for real predictive skill
Because regulators require it
Because it makes training faster
questions.explain: With faint signal and shifting regimes, ordinary validation approaches are especially prone to producing backtests that look great but have no real predictive power going forward.
